frontmatter_description: Identify the power, status, expertise, or institutional role structure between interaction partners without choosing what they should say or do.
title: Power, Status, and Role
use_when: Use when the question asks who has authority, rank, expertise, or role-based control in an interaction, or which party is responsible for which part of a task.
Use when labels such as teacher/student, manager/employee, doctor/patient, expert/novice, host/guest, parent/child, officer/citizen, or senior/junior shape how the scene is interpreted.
Use when the answer depends on whether the relation is hierarchical, peer-to-peer, advisory, supervisory, service-based, or dependency-based.
Use when a social norm follows from position or role rather than from personal liking, fairness, trust history, or group identity.
do_not_use_when: Do not use to pick what someone should SAY or DO given a power gap (comply, defer, push back, escalate, persuade, apologize); this unit only NAMES the structure - acting within it is choosing a communication move across a power gap, the power-navigation / hierarchical-communication capability.
Do not use when the variable is whether the relation is in-group/out-group, stereotype, belonging, or shared identity membership rather than rank or authority; that is group-identity reasoning.
Do not use when the task is adapting wording to a listener's level or background; that is audience calibration.
Do not use when the main variable is whether someone is reliable or honest over time; use trust and reputation reasoning.
Do not use when the main variable is whether a resource split, repayment, or burden is fair; use fairness and reciprocity reasoning.
Do not use when the main variable is whether information should be kept private or disclosed; use privacy, secrets, and boundaries reasoning.
trigger_checklist: Are there explicit role labels such as boss, teacher, doctor, client, officer, parent, expert, trainee, host, or guest?
Does one person have formal authority to evaluate, permit, assign, discipline, grade, hire, pay, treat, or enforce?
Does one person have recognized expertise or gatekeeping power even without formal rank?
Does the question ask how status, rank, role obligation, or institutional position changes interpretation?
Would the answer remain mostly the same if personal friendship, liking, or prior trust history were removed?
workflow: Confirm the question is asking WHO occupies WHICH role or WHO holds authority/responsibility, not what anyone should say or do. If it asks for a move (persuade, defer, push back, comply, apologize), stop and hand off after step 5.
List the interaction partners and every explicit title, role, institutional setting, or assigned task responsibility in the scene (e.g. team leader, the technical part, the market analysis).
Identify the source of asymmetry for each pair: formal authority, recognized expertise, dependency, seniority, service role, caregiving role, or temporary situational control (chair, host, captain).

Classify the relation as hierarchical, expert-novice, caregiver-dependent, service-provider/client, host-guest, peer, or unclear/mixed. Use only scene evidence; do not infer authority from who is louder, older, richer, or more confident.

Separate role from behavior quality and from familiarity: a rude manager is still a manager, a kind teacher is still an evaluator, and a friendly tone does not suspend evaluation, permission, or supervision power.

State only the role-based relation and the norm it activates (deference, duty of care, evaluation power, permission control, confidentiality expectation, obligation to follow instructions). Do NOT draft a reply or pick a tactic - that is choosing a communication move across a power gap, a separate task.

special_case.title: Informal familiarity does not erase formal role
special_case.rule: When people are friendly or familiar but one still holds institutional authority or expert responsibility, preserve the formal role unless the scene explicitly suspends it.

worked_example.scene: A student jokes casually with her professor after class, then asks whether she can submit the assignment late.
worked_example.question: What role structure matters here?
worked_example.answer_logic: Even though the tone is friendly, the professor still has evaluator and permission-granting authority over the student. The relevant structure is teacher/student with formal academic authority.

boundary_exit_rule: If the task asks what the lower- or higher-status person should say or do given the power gap (defer, push back, escalate, persuade, comply), name the role here, then exit to choosing a communication move across a power gap.
If the task is about wording the message to fit the listener's level or background, exit to audience calibration.
If the task asks whether an identity category, stereotype, or group belonging (same club, culture, team) explains interpretation rather than rank, exit to group identity.
If the task asks whether the person deserves trust because of past actions, exit to trust and reputation reasoning.
If the task asks whether someone took advantage, owed repayment, or split benefits unfairly, exit to fairness and reciprocity reasoning.
If the task asks whether a secret, medical fact, salary, grade, or personal detail may be shared, exit to privacy, secrets, and boundaries reasoning.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when the narrow diagnostic question is: what role, rank, authority, expertise, or status relation exists between the people, or which party is responsible for which part? It NAMES the structure; it never picks a move.
hard_boundary: This unit names the structure; it does not generate a tactful response or pick a strategy. Choosing what to say or do across a power gap (defer, push back, persuade, escalate) is the power-navigation / hierarchical-communication capability.
This unit reads rank, authority, expertise, and assigned responsibility; it does not read group belonging or stereotypes, which is group identity.
This unit does not evaluate moral fairness except where role duties define who has authority or obligation.
This unit does not infer loyalty, reliability, or betrayal from relationship history, and does not decide disclosure boundaries.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume the louder, older, richer, or more confident person has authority unless the scene gives a role-based reason.
Do not collapse expertise into trustworthiness; an expert role indicates knowledge authority, not necessarily honesty or goodwill.
Do not treat friendliness as equality when formal evaluation, permission, or supervision remains active.
common_failure_modes: Jumping to advice on HOW to speak to a boss (defer, push back, persuade) instead of just naming the boss/subordinate structure - that is choosing a communication move across a power gap.
Inferring authority from who is louder, older, richer, or more confident when the scene gives no role-based reason.
Mistaking shared group membership (same club, culture, or team) for a rank or authority relation, which is group identity.
Missing temporary situational authority such as a team captain, meeting chair, event host, or safety officer.
Letting a friendly or joking tone erase a still-active evaluation, permission, or supervision role.
Confusing role power with personal preference or popularity.

minimal_pair.case: A new analyst is unsure whether the team leader or the senior deputy outranks them on assigning a task; the question asks who holds the authority to assign it.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The pivot is NAMING who holds assignment authority - the role/rank structure itself. Stays in this unit.

minimal_pair.case: Same office, but now the question is how the new analyst should respond when the team leader assigns them the deputy's usual task without seeming to overstep.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: Single variable flipped from identify to act: the structure is given and the task is now choosing a communication move across the power gap. Routes away.

boundary_stress_test: A CEO and an intern play on the same weekend soccer team: identify whether the workplace hierarchy is active in the current scene or whether they are temporary teammates.
A junior engineer corrects a senior manager about a technical bug: separate organizational rank from domain expertise.
A teacher asks a student for help fixing a projector: the student may have technical expertise, but the teacher still holds classroom authority.
A customer yells at a cashier: customer status gives service-role expectations, not unlimited authority over the employee.
references.generalization_note: Role structure is a social-cognitive frame for interpreting obligations, authority, deference, permission, evaluation, expertise, and assigned responsibility. Diagnose it from explicit roles and situational powers, then hand off: choosing what to say or do across the gap is the power-navigation / hierarchical-communication capability, tailoring wording to the listener is audience calibration, and group belonging or stereotype is group identity.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A scene names or implies roles such as manager/employee, teacher/student, expert/novice, or officer/citizen, and the question asks what relationship, authority structure, or assigned responsibility matters.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: A scene shows a confident, older, or loud person giving orders, but no role-based authority is established; the trap is inferring rank from manner instead of evidence.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: A scene involves a clear hierarchy plus a request for what someone should say or do; this unit may name the hierarchy but must hand the move-choice to the power-navigation / hierarchical-communication capability.

notes: Keep the output focused on role diagnosis, not social strategy.
Use evidence from the scene rather than stereotypes about age, gender, class, profession, or culture.
Mixed structures are allowed: one person may have formal rank while the other has domain expertise.
core_question: Identify teacher/student, manager/subordinate, expert/novice, and related role structures
